text: Chapter 4 derived Grover's algorithm in full. This lesson puts its real, verified numbers next to classical search's real numbers, side by side, and applies the honesty checklist from the previous lesson to the comparison.

For unstructured search over N equals 8 items with exactly one marked item and no structure to exploit, the only guaranteed classical strategy is checking one at a time. Worst case, 8 checks, if the marked item happens to be checked last. Average case, N plus 1 over 2, which is 4.5 checks. That's the real number Grover's result has to beat — not a strawman, the best honest classical strategy available.

Chapter 4's verified table shows 2 Grover iterations deliver a 94.53% chance of success at N equals 8, against up to 8 classical checks worst case or 4.5 average. Scaling up: at N equals 16, Grover needs 3 calls against 16 worst case; at N equals one million, Grover needs 785 calls against a million. Every one of these is an actual floor computation of pi over 4 times root N, and the gap widens exactly as root N versus N.

Applying the checklist: rule 2 says the oracle call isn't free — it's a real quantum circuit whose gate count depends on the specific problem. Rule 4 says the moment any structure exists, a sorted array or a hash table, classical computing wins outright with no quantum hardware at all. Rule 5 says the 94.53% figure comes from a noiseless simulation, and real hardware errors will lower it. None of this makes Grover's algorithm fake — it makes the honest claim narrower than quantum computers search databases faster.
